opus-5.5.text:
I think people mostly evaluated long context on the wrong axis. The early framing was "you can stuff a whole book in and ask a question about it," which sounds like a retrieval convenience. What it actually gives you is a lot more interesting: it's a form of learning that happens at inference time.

When you put a few hundred thousand tokens of a codebase, or an obscure language's grammar, or a pile of research papers into context, the model's performance on that task jumps dramatically. Sometimes it goes from basically useless to roughly expert-level within a single forward pass. That's in-context learning doing something that would otherwise require fine-tuning, and it's far more sample efficient than gradient descent. So you get a really cheap, really fast way to specialize a general model to your exact situation.

The second reason is what it means for agents. A lot of what stops models from doing long-horizon work isn't raw intelligence on any single step, it's the ability to hold everything relevant in their heads at once: what they've tried, what failed, the state of the codebase, the instructions from three hours ago. Humans have a pretty tiny working memory, maybe a handful of items, and we compensate with notes and external tools. Models can have a working memory of millions of tokens. That's a genuinely superhuman capability and I don't think people have priced in how much it matters once reliability on each step gets high enough to chain long tasks together.

And third, there's a nice interaction with the reliability point. Each extra "nine" of per-step accuracy compounds over long tasks, and long context is part of what lets you actually exploit that, because the model isn't losing the thread. So you might see what looks like a sudden jump in agentic capability that's really just these two curves crossing.

So I'd say it's underhyped because people see it as a feature, "bigger input window," when it's closer to a new learning mechanism plus a massive working memory, and both of those feed directly into the things we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response says that putting a codebase into context can rapidly specialize the model to that situation, even moving it toward expert-level performance in one forward pass. This communicates near-instant onboarding.

r002.rationale: The response describes a performance jump from hundreds of thousands of tokens of context, but does not mention improved next-token prediction or compare the gain to a large increase in model scale.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people got a little bit lost in the discourse around benchmark numbers and the kind of "needle in a haystack" demos, and they missed the thing that actually matters, which is that long context changes what the model fundamentally is.

Think about what we were doing before. You had a model that had a fixed, frozen snapshot of knowledge from pretraining, and then you had this tiny window, a few thousand tokens, where you could tell it something new. Everything else had to go through fine-tuning or retrieval, and both of those are lossy. Retrieval is you guessing which chunks are relevant before the model has even looked at the problem. Fine-tuning is slow, expensive, and kind of blunt. So the model's ability to actually learn about your specific situation, your codebase, your company, your life, was incredibly constrained.

With long context, you can just put the whole thing in. The entire repository. Every email thread. The full history of a project. And the thing that's underappreciated is that in-context learning is really, really sample efficient compared to gradient descent. Models pick things up from a handful of examples in context that would take thousands of examples to instill through training. So when you give a model a million tokens of context, you're not just giving it more facts to look up, you're giving it the ability to adapt to a distribution it has never seen before, on the fly, at inference time.

That's a qualitative shift. It's the difference between a very knowledgeable stranger and someone who has actually been working alongside you for months. And I think the reason it's underhyped is that the demos were things like "find the random sentence I hid in a book," which is impressive but kind of misses the point. The point is the model reasoning over all of it at once, drawing connections between the thing on page three and the thing on page nine hundred, and doing that reliably.

The other piece is that this is what makes agents actually work. If you want a model to go do a long, multi-step task, it needs to hold the whole trajectory in its head. What it tried, what failed, what it learned along the way. If you're constantly summarizing and throwing things away, you're compounding errors. Long context lets you keep the full state.

And honestly, I think the capability is ahead of what people have figured out how to use it for. There's a lag between a capability existing and the applications catching up, and I think we're still in that lag for long context.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can take in an entire codebase and adapt to it on the fly at inference time, describing a shift from stranger to someone who has worked alongside you for months. This communicates near-instant onboarding through context.

r002.rationale: The response discusses long context and codebases but does not say that millions of code tokens improve next-token prediction or that the improvement is comparable to increasing model scale.

astra-6.text:
I think people tend to imagine long context as, “I can put a really long PDF in and ask questions about it.” But the more interesting implication is that the model can have all the context you have when you do your job.

If you hire someone, you don’t expect them to be maximally useful from the first conversation. They need to read the codebase, understand the decisions people made, see examples of what good work looks like, and learn what you care about. A lot of that is information that isn’t in the task description. With a sufficiently long context, you can give a model that background instead of trying to compress everything into a perfectly specified prompt.

And that changes what you can delegate. Rather than asking a little isolated question, you can say, “Here’s the project, here’s everything we’ve tried, here’s what we’re trying to accomplish. Work out the next step.”

The caveat is that fitting information into the context window isn’t the same as using it well. The model has to connect things that are far apart and pick out what matters. But if that works, long context starts to look less like a document feature and more like a way to give the model experience with your particular problem. I think that’s a much bigger deal.

r001.rationale: The response says long context can give a model background about a project, but it does not state that this solves onboarding almost instantly.

r002.rationale: It does not mention millions of codebase tokens, improved next-token prediction, or an effect comparable to scaling up the model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people tend to think of long context as, “Great, I can put a longer PDF in there.” But the more interesting thing is that you can give the model all the information it needs to do a task, including information you wouldn’t have known to retrieve in advance.

Take working in a codebase. A lot of the difficulty is understanding how everything fits together: why someone made a particular decision, what conventions they use, what other things will break if you change this function. If you can fit the whole codebase, the documentation, and the history of what you’ve tried into context, that’s a very different experience from asking a model a question with a few retrieved snippets.

And there’s an in-context learning angle. You can show it hundreds of examples of how you want something done instead of trying to specify everything in a prompt or doing a fine-tuning run. You’re effectively giving it experience with the task.

The caveat is that accepting a million tokens isn’t the same as using a million tokens well. The model has to connect information across that context, and it has to be cheap and fast enough to be useful. But if you get those things right, I think it changes the kinds of work you can delegate, rather than just the length of the documents you can summarize.

r001.rationale: The response describes giving a model a whole codebase, documentation, and history, but does not say this solves onboarding almost instantly.

r002.rationale: It mentions fitting a codebase into context, but does not state that millions of tokens improve next-token prediction comparably to a large increase in model scale.
